title: Support automation that does not sound like a script
metaTitle: Customer support automation UX, in voice
excerpt: Support automation should use the brand's real sentences and offer a person when the question leaves the script. Do not give the bot an employee name.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The reply being typed is the kind of sentence support should sound like, without a fictional employee.
caption: A reply written in a real voice, at a real desk. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should support automation sound?
faqs.answer: Use the sentences the company is willing to say, written by hand for the questions that have a reliable source. Be specific: the date, the amount, the next step. Skip a fictional employee name, a portrait, and a scripted apology that appears on every ticket.

faqs.question: When should a thread go to a person?
faqs.answer: Hand it over when the question leaves the source: damage, an unrecognized charge, an exception, or any promise the script is not allowed to make. Say that a person will take it, and say when, only if someone is staffed to do that. If the customer asks for a person, route the thread.

faqs.question: What should we look at after launch?
faqs.answer: Read threads for a customer who had to repeat the problem, and for a promise a person had to undo. Ten accurate replies are more useful than forty stale ones. When the policy changes, change the reply the same day, because the customer will treat the reply as the policy.

markdown:
Customer support automation UX should sound like the brand and know when to stop. Use the sentences the company is willing to say. Offer a person when the question leaves the script. Do not give the bot a human name, a portrait, or a backstory. Pretending it is an employee is how a routine reply becomes a breach of trust.

People write to support because something is stuck. They can accept a direct answer from a system. They should not have to wonder whether a person ignored them.

## Start from the sentences you already mean

A support flow needs a verbal identity before it needs a model. Three sentences the company will say, and three it will not, are enough to steer every template. The yes list might be plain, specific, and willing to admit a limit. The no list might be jokes during a billing problem, fake certainty, and blame pointed at the customer.

Write the common replies from that list, by hand, before you automate anything. Order status. Password reset. Refund window. Where to send a file. Each reply names the fact, the next step, and the way to reach a person if the fact does not fit. Those replies are the script. Automation may deliver them. It should not improvise a new policy in a friendlier voice.

If you do not have the sentences yet, stop and write them. A model will otherwise supply the voice of a generic help desk, and that voice will be the brand on the worst day of the customer's week.

## The script, and the door out of it

Map the questions that have a reliable source. The order system knows the status. The policy page knows the refund window. The bot, or the canned reply, may answer those by reading the source and using your sentences. Show the fact. "Your order shipped on Tuesday, and the tracking link is below." That is a human-sounding reply because it is specific, not because it says it hopes you are having a great day.

Map the questions that leave the source. A damaged good, a charge the customer does not recognize, an exception to the policy, anything angry, anything that requires a promise. These get one move: acknowledge the topic, say a person will take it, and say when. The acknowledgment can be automated. The promise of a person has to be staffed. An automated "I've escalated this" that lands in an unattended queue is a script pretending to be care.

Do not trap people. Every automated turn includes the way out, in text, not only behind a menu. "Reply 'person' or write to this address." If they ask for a person twice, the system stops pitching answers and routes the thread. Arguing someone out of the request is the behavior people mean when they say support sounds like a script.

The W3C notes that the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) apply to AI web interfaces, and that understandable and operable are part of the standard. A support widget people must use should name its actions and keep the replies readable. The way out is an operation, not a courtesy. If it cannot be reached and understood, the automation is not finished.

## Voice without a costume

Short sentences. The customer's words where you can reflect the actual problem. No exclamation points as a substitute for help. No "as an AI" essay, and no borrowed first name.

A named employee is a person who can be accountable. A bot named "Sam" with a face is a fiction, and it makes the door to a real person feel like a downgrade. Call it what it is: the help assistant, or simply the replies from the company. When a person takes over, sign with a real name and do not imply they were there the whole time.

Templates can include a blank the system fills from the record, such as the order number or the first name on the account. They should not include a blank for empathy theater. "I totally understand how frustrating it must be to..." on every ticket is how a script announces itself. Specifics are the empathy that holds up. The date, the amount, the next step.

An example, labeled as an exercise: a brand shop's assistant answers "where is my order" from the shipping record, in two sentences, with the link. It answers "this arrived damaged" with "A person on the team will look at this today. You can add a photo to this thread." It does not offer a partial refund on its own. The refund is a pay decision, and it waits for the person.

## What to measure

Read the threads. The measure of the voice is whether a customer had to repeat themselves, and whether a person had to undo a promise the automation made. Count those. A high deflection number, with threads full of repeated questions, means the script is winning a metric and losing the conversation.

Keep the script short enough to maintain. Ten accurate replies beat forty stale ones. When the policy changes, the reply changes the same day, because the reply is now the policy as far as the customer is concerned.

Read five real threads a week, including ones that looked "deflected." You are looking for a customer who had to restate the problem, a promise the script was not allowed to make, and a door to a person that did not open. Fix the reply that caused it before you add a new topic. A support flow improves by editing sentences, not by adding another layer of automation on top of a reply that already confused someone.

The sentences themselves belong to the brand, not only to the help desk. The piece on choosing what the company will and will not say is [verbal identity](/blog/verbal-identity). Support is where a sloppy voice becomes expensive.
